---
title: "Jobs, Not Jam"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
**Prerequisites:** Login Node Manners and Grow the Carapace. **Objective:** let the agent draft job scripts while you keep submitting and cancelling under your own approval, and know what polling costs.
**Time:** about 20 minutes. <span class="ao-badge">Last verified (docs, not run): Slurm, Claude Code and OpenCode (V2) docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in `research/hpc-and-notebooks.md`)</span>
:::

Whether an agent should be anywhere near your cluster account is a decision for you and your cluster staff. **Follow your own cluster's policy and data agreement over this page.** Nothing here says that agent use is allowed or expected on any cluster. This quest is laptop-only reading: never try the rules on a real cluster to see what happens.

## Draft versus submit

A job script is text. Letting an agent *draft* one is low risk, because you read it before anything runs. *Submitting* spends shared resources, and cancelling can destroy work. A sensible split:

- the agent drafts scripts, and may check state (`squeue`, `sinfo`, `sacct`). *General practice:* limit `sacct` with `-j <jobid>` or `-S <start date>` so it does not dump the whole accounting history
- you approve `sbatch`, `srun`, `salloc` and `scancel`

Before approving an `sbatch`, read the script and the resource request: `--time`, `--mem`, and the array size if it is an array.

## The permission rules

Rules are enforced by the harness, with deny before ask before allow.

::: {.panel-tabset group="companion"}

## Claude Code

A teaching configuration, derived from the permission rules in the docs rather than copied from them:

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(squeue *)", "Bash(sinfo *)", "Bash(sacct *)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(sbatch *)", "Bash(srun *)", "Bash(salloc *)", "Bash(scancel *)"],
    "deny":  ["Bash(scancel -u *)", "Bash(scancel --user*)"]
  }
}
```

An `ask` rule prompts even when a narrower `allow` rule matches. Ask and deny rules apply to every part of a compound command (`&&`, `;`, `|`, loops, `$(...)`).

**The caveat:** the docs say Bash rules are not a security boundary. `Bash(rm *)` does not stop `/bin/rm` or `bash -c 'rm ...'`, and by the same logic a `scancel` rule is not watertight. For real enforcement use a PreToolUse hook (the sandbox limits files and network, not Slurm commands). Treat the rules above as a prompt that keeps you in the loop, not as a lock.

## OpenCode + Ollama

OpenCode (V2 docs; check your installed version) accepts `allow`, `ask` and `deny`, and an unmatched action asks. But per the docs its base policy begins with an allow-all rule, so `sbatch` is likely to run unprompted; confirm in your version. Add this to the permissions array in `opencode.jsonc`:

```json
"permissions": [
  { "action": "shell", "resource": "sbatch *", "effect": "ask" }
]
```

Add similar rules for `srun`, `salloc` and `scancel`, and a `deny` for `scancel -u *`. Rules are ordered, so check where they sit relative to the broad allow. As in Claude Code, a rule that fails to match does not stop a destructive command: shell rules are not a sandbox.

:::

## Why `scancel -u` is the dangerous one

`scancel -u <you>` signals **all** your jobs, not just the ones the agent submitted. Whole jobs are terminated, and other work of yours dies with them. The other bulk filters, `-n` (name), `-t` (state) and `-p` (partition), also act on many jobs at once, so they belong under `ask` too (the `scancel *` rule above already covers them). Prefer `scancel <jobid>` for an ID the agent itself submitted. Slurm can also rate-limit requests per user when they come in at a sustained high rate, so a runaway loop of commands is a problem for the scheduler as well as for you.

## Polling costs money, and attention

Claude Code charges by token use. The whole conversation is sent with every request, and each tool use sends another request. A `/loop` (a command that re-runs a prompt on a timer) that polls `squeue` keeps firing on its interval, even while the session is idle, and sends your full context each time. Verbose output such as long logs also inflates the context.

*General practice:* poll at intervals of minutes, not seconds, and read job output files or use `sacct` instead of watching the queue. Do not `/loop` a `squeue` poll.

From the Claude Code docs: foreground commands time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so an agent waiting on a long foreground command, such as an `srun` that blocks until it finishes, gets cut off.

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [sbatch](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html): SchedMD (Slurm), docs. Why read: it is the manual for submitting jobs, including --test-only to validate a request without submitting.
- [scancel](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scancel.html): SchedMD (Slurm), docs. Why read: it shows that user and state filters cancel everything they match, so an agent's cleanup can kill your other jobs.
- [High Throughput Computing Administration Guide](https://slurm.schedmd.com/high_throughput.html): SchedMD (Slurm), docs. Why read: it is an administrator guide that mentions per-user rate limits on scheduler requests; read it for why floods of commands matter, not as user advice.
- [Configure permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows allow, ask and deny rules (for example asking before sbatch) and warns that Bash rules are not a security boundary.
:::
